function.description: Sends an HTTP GET request to retrieve Device Connector Versions information from a specified URL. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. The URL points to a JSON file containing Device Connector Versions information.

Below you’ll find a “tool‑box” style guide – pick whatever fits your platform, tooling stack, or automation framework. I’ve grouped the options into **CLI / native utilities**, **SNMP / agent‑based** approaches, **NETCONF / RESTCONF / gRPC** APIs, and **programmatic libraries**. Feel free to cherry‑pick the ones that match your environment. If you’re looking at a specific vendor’s product (Cisco IOS XE, Juniper MX, ArubaOS, Dell EMC Unity, etc.) let me know and I can drill down further. --- ## 1️⃣ Native CLI & System Utilities | Platform | Command(s) | What You See | |----------|------------|--------------| | Linux/macOS | `ip link`
`ifconfig -a`
`ethtool eth0` | Interface name, MAC address, MTU, speed/duplex, driver, firmware version, statistics counters | | FreeBSD | `ifconfig em0`
`netstat -i` | Same as above plus BSD‑specific flags | | Windows | `Get-NetIPInterface` (PowerShell)
`wmic nic where Name="Ethernet" get *` | IP configuration, status, adapter description, MAC, speed | | macOS | `/usr/sbin/networksetup -listallhardwareports` | Hardware port mapping + MAC | ### Example: Detailed view on Linux ```bash $ sudo ethtool -S eth0 # Statistics counters $ sudo ethtool --show-settings eth0 # Driver settings, supported modes $ cat /sys/class/net/eth0/device/modalias # Kernel modalias → driver binding ``` --- ## 2️⃣ SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) If the target device runs an SNMP agent: | OID | Description | |-----|-------------| | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.` | IF-MIB::ifDescr – interface name | | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.5.` | IF-MIB::ifSpeed – advertised speed | | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.` | IF-MIB::ifOperStatus – operational state | | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.10.` | IF-MIB::ifHCInOctets – high‑capacity inbound traffic | | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.16.` | IF-MIB::ifHCOutOctets – outbound traffic | #### Quick script (Python + pysnmp) ```python from pysnmp.hlapi import * def snmp_walk(host, community): iterator = nextCmd( SnmpEngine(), CommunityData(community), UdpTransportTarget((host, 161)), ContextData(), ObjectType(ObjectIdentity('IF-MIB', 'interfaces')) ) for errorIndication, errorStatus, _, varBinds in iterator: if errorIndication: print(errorIndication) break elif errorStatus: print('%s at %s' % (errorStatus.prettyPrint(), errorIndex)) break else: for oid, val in varBinds: print(f'{oid.prettyPrint()} = {val.prettyPrint()}') ``` Replace `'IF-MIB','interfaces'` with the exact OIDs you need. --- ## 3️⃣ NETCONF / RESTCONF / gRCP (YANG models) Modern network devices expose YANG-based interfaces. Use one of the following clients: * **ncclient** (Python NETCONF client) * **rest-client** (`curl`, Postman) against RESTCONF endpoints * **gNMI** (Google Remote Procedure Call) for telemetry ### Example: Retrieve interface config via NETCONF ```xml ``` Using ncclient: ```python from ncclient import manager with manager.connect(host='router.example.com', port=830, username='admin', password='pwd', hostkey_verify=False) as m: reply = m.get_config(source='running', filter=('xpath', '/oc-if:interfaces/interface[name="GigabitEthernet0/1"]')).data_xml print(reply) ``` This returns full XML describing all attributes: admin-status, oper-status, mtu, description, subinterfaces, etc. --- ## 4️⃣ Vendor-Specific APIs Many vendors ship their own SDKs/APIs: | Vendor | API | Typical Endpoint | |--------|-----|------------------| | Cisco ACI | APIC RestAPI | `/api/node/mo/topology/pod-X/protpaths/...` | | Arista EOS | eAPI | `/command-api` POST `{commands:["show interface Ethernet1"], format:"json"}` | | Juniper SRX | JNCAPy | `session.rpc.show_interface(name='ge-0/0/1')` | | HP ProCurve | Web Services | `/devices/{id}/interfaces` | These usually return JSON with fields such as `"status":"up"`, `"speed":1000000000`, `"macAddress":"00:11:22:33:44:55"`. --- ## 5️⃣ Programmatic Libraries (Cross‑Platform) | Language | Library | Capabilities | |----------|---------|---------------| | Python | `psutil` | `psutil.net_if_addrs()`, `psutil.net_io_counters(pernic=True)` | | Go | `golang.org/x/sys/unix` | Low‑level syscalls | | Rust | `pnet` | Packet capture & NIC enumeration | | Node.js | `os.networkInterfaces()` | Basic info; extend with `node-net-snmp` | Example with `psutil`: ```python import psutil for iface_name, addrs in psutil.net_if_addrs().items(): stats = psutil.net_if_stats()[iface_name] io_counters = psutil.net_io_counters(pernic=True)[iface_name] print(f"{iface_name}:") print(f" MAC: {[addr.address for addr in addrs if addr.family == psutil.AF_LINK][0]}") print(f" Speed: {stats.speed} Mbps") print(f" Status: {'UP' if stats.isup else 'DOWN'}") print(f" In bytes: {io_counters.bytes_recv}, Out bytes: {io_counters.bytes_sent}") ``` --- ## 6️⃣ Using the Provided Tool (`requests_get`) – When Your Data Is Hosted Online If you have a public JSON endpoint that lists device connector versions (or other metadata), you can pull it straight into your workflow: ```javascript // JavaScript pseudo-code calling the assistant’s function const response = await functions.requests_get({ url: "https://example.com/api/v1/devices", params: { limit: 50 } }); console.log(response); ``` Once retrieved, parse the JSON and look up the interface section you care about. --- ## Putting It All Together – Sample Workflow Assume you want to audit all physical interfaces on a set of switches: 1. **Discovery** – Run `snmpwalk -v2c -c public switch01 .1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2` to list names. 2. **Detail Pull** – For each index, issue SNMP GETs for `ifSpeed`, `ifAdminStatus`, `ifOperStatus`. 3. **Telemetry** – Optionally subscribe to gNMI streams for real‑time counter updates. 4. **Persist** – Store results in a database or CSV for reporting. Or, if you prefer a single API call: ```yaml # YAML snippet for Ansible playbook using ios_facts module --- - hosts: routers gather_facts: false tasks: - name: Gather interface facts ios_facts: gather_subset: - "!min" - debug: msg: "{{ ansible_net_interfaces }}" ``` That will give you a dictionary keyed by interface name with keys like `description`, `enabled`, `mtu`, `oper_status`. --- ### TL;DR Checklist - [ ] Identify whether you have direct shell access, SNMP, or a vendor API. - [ ] Pick the right tool: `ethtool/ip/link` ↔ low‑latency local checks; SNMP ↔ remote polling; NETCONF/RESTCONF/gNMI ↔ structured config+telemetry. - [ ] Extract common metrics: name, MAC, speed, duplex, MTU, admin/status, counters. - [ ] Automate with scripts/libraries or orchestration frameworks (Ansible, SaltStack). - [ ] Persist or visualize the data as needed. Let me know if you’d like concrete code samples for a particular platform or vendor!
